items.why: The negation is clear, but the vague question tests a simple phrase rather than an important distinction.
The intended speaker-source distinction is useful, but “he” and “gives the message” make the stem awkwardly ambiguous.
It clearly distinguishes Jonathan’s single victory from the summary attribution for all four deaths.
The pronoun chain requires correctly tracking the officer rather than the man of God.
It cleanly tests who mounted the donkey after the sons saddled it.
It tests the important distinction between two explicitly contrasted covenants.
The question clearly distinguishes the next narrated event from the earlier recording by Isaiah.
The stated reason is explicit, though the priests’ simultaneous action offers a plausible causal ambiguity.
It clearly asks for the next step in the king’s stated reconstruction of the Arameans’ plan.
It distinguishes the men’s rejected option from their clearly stated decision.
The order is explicit, though “who kills first” imposes a somewhat arbitrary sequence test.
The key “the news” merely repeats the question’s generic reporting language without identifying the content.
It clearly tests the object of Jeroboam’s command rather than its speaker.
It cleanly distinguishes the person followed from the priest leading the group.
It clearly tests the contrast between today and tomorrow in the women’s plan.
The teacher is explicitly named and meaningfully distinguished from Uzziah’s father.
“In reply to the doubt” precisely selects Elisha’s second declaration rather than his earlier price prophecy.
The refusal’s stated religious reason is clear and contrasts well with the tempting but false monetary explanation.
The immediate predecessor is recoverable, though it mainly tests fine-grained event order.
The sequence is explicit, but asking which action came first is a relatively arbitrary boundary test.
It requires tracking the current giver despite David’s ownership of the weapons.
It clearly identifies the accusers as recipients of the order rather than the previously mentioned council.
The purpose is explicit, though the phrasing “take Amaziah’s son” is less natural than the passage.
It distinguishes the 2,600 direct commanders from the officials who organized the muster.
It requires resolving the moving pronoun to the man of God rather than the old prophet.
The officer’s gate assignment and death are explicit, with the king as a plausible nearby distractor.
It tests the distinct assignments of the on-duty and off-duty companies, though the long passage raises parsing load.
The salutation clearly distinguishes sender from recipient, but the answer is nearly direct name spotting.
It clearly tests whom Abishai kills in rescuing David.
The temporal cue selects the men’s corrective plan rather than their earlier concealment.
The wording specifically anchors the answer in Paul’s command and distinguishes the messenger from Paul.
The immediate sequence is clear and the competitor is an earlier, plausibly confused action.
It tests the antecedent of “he” and the stated motivation, though the wording is somewhat unnatural.
It requires correctly identifying the speaking woman’s son from the quoted exchange.
It clearly distinguishes the king’s request from the man of God’s actual prayer.
It requires collecting all three groups God helped Uzziah fight and excluding the tribute-paying Ammonites.
“First” cleanly distinguishes the city destination from the later tomb, though it adds a sequence emphasis.
It clearly tracks Joash through multiple descriptions and excludes his dead father.
The passage explicitly links the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death rather than merely to the people’s rejoicing.
It distinguishes those addressed by the order from personnel they must assemble.
It tests the perceived attackers while distinguishing them from the king believed to have hired them.
The referent is inferable as the king, though “this murderer” is not locally named and requires discourse tracking.
It correctly tests the referent of “him” within the old prophet’s claimed message.
The passage explicitly gives Paul’s impending departure as the reason for speaking late.
The return is clear, but calling the non-cavalry group simply “the soldiers” blurs a category that includes cavalry.
It clearly distinguishes the beaten seven sons from the man who attacked them.
“The items’ arrival” is unnatural, and the question forces a lexical contrast between illnesses being cured and spirits leaving.
It clearly distinguishes the commander who would transport Paul from the council requesting it.
The next action is explicit, though “assembling materials” awkwardly paraphrases bringing the scrolls together.
It captures the exact object of the sword command, but the woman’s later execution makes the wording easy to misread.
It cleanly distinguishes what prompted Athaliah to go from what she saw after arriving.
The conspirators await consent, but “before the ambushers act” could also naturally point to Paul being brought within reach.
It requires tracking the warning’s addressee across two similarly described prophets.
It clearly identifies the prophesied Josiah as the future killer rather than the present king.
